significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish that when belief and assertion diverge, "there exists a linear probe over intermediate activations" whose cross-topic and cross-elicitation performance exceeds output-based lie detection: primarily a form-(i) decodability claim with a limited form-(iii) comparative relation between detector performances, not a causal mechanism of deception. It establishes a potentially useful phenomenon—cross-context latent-deception decodability—but neither identifies components that produce deceptive behavior nor explains why the signature arises; it would nevertheless constrain detector selection in light of the black-box approach of Pacchiardi et al. (ICLR 2024) and the persistence of deceptive policies under safety training reported by Hubinger et al. (2024). A verified-false result would informatively reject a context-general linear signature or its claimed advantage over output detection, although it would not rule out nonlinear, model-specific, or naturally emergent deception signals; true and false therefore denote distinguishable states. After topic substitution, generic mechanistic work on LLM safety would not earn this score—the specific belief-assertion divergence and cross-context detector ranking provide the increment—but the result remains close to the topic's standard probe-based hypothesis rather than a load-bearing causal law.

reach.justification: The transferable handle named by the claim is a "linear probe over intermediate activations" for distinguishing "sincere from deceptive generation," with probe score/AUROC serving as an internal diagnostic that auditors could use. It is mainly concurrent or post hoc rather than ex ante: activations are read "at the point of assertion," so the claim does not forecast deception before generation begins, though an implementation could potentially gate an assertion before release. Its asserted scope spans "topics and elicitation methods," but not model families, architectures, or training regimes; after re-extraction on a new model, the conclusion predicts only that one should look for a linear signature, not its direction, magnitude, or a quantitative relation that must recur. The topic-substitution check lowers rather than supports the rating—LLM safety alone supplies no reusable handle—while this particular probe could reach deployment auditors beyond the immediate research line, albeit with limited transfer under the explicitly anticipated "adaptive evasion."
